newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic ally backs opposition claims, reforms.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic ally backs opposition claims, reforms.

text.p: A moderate party leader within Serbia's ruling leftist coalition called on Thursday for swift restoration of opposition election wins and economic reforms to resolve the country's worst political crisis in a decade.

"The current political crisis has long eclipsed the reason which provoked it, but the immense damage to Serbia testifies to a foolish, irresponsible policy," Dusan Mihajlovic, leader of the New Democracy Party, told Reuters in an interview.
"We have a saying: "You don't kill a whole ox for a pound of beef."

Mihajlovic was referring to the political crisis that erupted after the ruling Socialists and neo-communists annulled election victories in November by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition in 14 cities including Belgrade.

In protest Zajedno has brought up to half a million supporters into the streets every day for the past nine weeks in the biggest challenge yet to the 10-year rule of strongman President Slobodan Milosevic.
The West, spearheaded by the United States, has sharply condemned Milosevic's conduct. Washington has threatened further sanctions against Belgrade unless it improves its human rights record.

New Democracy, a moderate voice in Milosevic's autocratic coalition which also includes the Socialist Party (SPS) and the neocommunist Yugoslav United Left (JUL), has broken ranks with its larger partners' hardline approach to the protests.
It has emerged from the crisis as a palatable alternative to the corruption-ridden and power-hungry SPS and JUL.
"New Democracy has said from the outset that the will of the voters must not be changed, that it must be respected," Mihajlovic said.
"We believe the best way to solve the acute crisis is for authorities and opposition to fully respect conclusions of the OSCE delegation.
"Independently of this, we think democratic reforms must be speeded up and that everything should be done for Yugoslavia to return to the international community," he said.
New Democracy is stuck in the middle of a pitched battle between moderates and hardliners in the ruling parties.

Milosevic has still not spoken out on the crisis. Analysts believe that New Democracy was opening a door but Milosevic has so far refused to walk through it despite increasing political and economic damage to the country.
"It is clear that this crisis has considerably slowed down Yugoslavia's reintegration process," Mihajlovic said.

He listed Washington's continuing sanctions, postponement of the European Union's restoration of Belgrade's preferential trade status, and a halt in talks on Yugoslavia's re-admission to the International Monetary Fund.
"We feel this crisis was unnecessary, provoked by irresponsible people in local SPS leaderships for no other reason but to avoid election defeat," he said.
Mihajlovic said the cost of their intransigence was huge but warned the price could go even higher.

"We think this is irresponsible political behaviour but the genie is out of the bottle now. It is of utmost importance not to lose control of events and to get out of everything in a peaceful way," Mihajlovic said.
He also warned that time was running out. "There are just a few days left for the mess to be sorted out."

He was referring to a European Union ministerial meeting in a few days and the inauguration of U.S. President Bill Clinton on January 20. Both events would pile more pressure on Milosevic to toe the pro-democracy line but it remained unclear whether he would heed the last calls to reason, he said.
